docs.title: PS Vita Porting Encyclopedia & Manual (SoLoader)
docs.text: Welcome to the English section of the PS Vita Porting Wiki. This compendium serves as an end-to-end engineering handbook and definitive technical reference for porting compiled Android applications (.apk / .so) into native PlayStation Vita homebrew executables (.vpk).

# Chapter Core Focus & Technical Depth 00 Fundamentals & Architecture ARMv7 Cortex-A9 CPU, PowerVR SGX543MP4+ GPU, CDRAM vs RAM partitions, SoLoader vs Emulation vs Static Recompilation. 01 Environment & Toolchains Setting up VitaSDK, vitaGL, kubridge, fd_fix, FalsoJNI, psvita-toolkit, Docker with headless Ghidra, jadx. 02 APK Triage & Viability Analysis Feasibility checks: ARMv7 vs 64-bit, GLES1 vs GLES2, STL dependencies, memory footprint, viability decision matrix. 03 Static Analysis & Reverse Engineering Java decompilation (jadx), pseudo-C extraction (Ghidra), symbol extraction with objdump and nm. 04 SoLoader Core & Relocations In-memory ELF layout, ARM relocation types (R_ARM_RELATIVE, R_ARM_GLOB_DAT), binary patching and symbol hooking. 05 FalsoJNI & Java Bridge Emulating JVM/JNIEnv, Android type signatures, Java callbacks, safe stubs vs game-freezing no-ops. 06 Graphics Pipeline with vitaGL vitaGL over SCE GXM, GLSL to Cg/GXP shader translation, FBOs, 960x544 scaling, premultiplied alpha, VRAM limits. 07 Audio Subsystem sceAudioOut, OpenAL-Soft for Vita, Vorbis/MP3 streaming, bridging AudioTrack, SoundPool, and MediaPlayer. 08 Controls & Input Mapping Front/Rear touch panels, buttons and analog sticks, preventing touch report ID heap corruption, touch-to-pad emulation. 09 File System & Assets Redirecting paths to ux0:data/, FAT/exFAT case insensitivity quirks, reading assets from ZIP/OBB in memory. 10 LiveArea & VPK Packaging Strict 8-bit indexed PNG rules (eliminating 0x8010113D), param.sfo, template.xml, cleaning macOS ._ junk files. 11 Crash Triage & Hardware Debugging Triangulation methodology: .psp2dmp analysis, vita-parse-core, PC vs LR, ARMv7 memory alignment traps (ldrd). 12 Real Engine Archaeology Production case studies from 30+ ports: Gameloft, Gamevil Nexus2/Clet, Com2uS, custom Cocos2d-x pipelines. 13 AI-Assisted Porting Guide Human + AI pair programming protocols, context and token economy, deterministic prompts for JNI stubs. 14 Base Guide (gl33ntwine) Vitaliy Atamanenko's original foundational guide with modern technical annotations and context. 15 Quick Reference & Cheat Sheets JNI signature tables, common VitaOS kernel error codes, Bionic libc to VitaSDK Newlib translation tables.

[!TIP] For New Developers: Start with Chapters 00, 01, and 02 before acquiring an APK. For Experienced Engineers / AI Agents: Chapters 04 (ELF Relocations), 05 (FalsoJNI), 06 (vitaGL), and 11 (Crash Triage) contain the core low-level logic required to resolve production hardware crashes.

docs.title: 00. Fundamentals & Architecture
docs.text: To master porting mobile games to the PlayStation Vita, one must understand both the console's physical hardware architecture and the theoretical foundation of the SoLoader methodology.

docs.title: 🔬 PS Vita Hardware Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "Sony CXD5315GG SoC"
        subgraph "CPU: ARM Cortex-A9 MPCore"
            Core0["Core 0 (App Main Thread)"]
            Core1["Core 1 (App Worker/Audio)"]
            Core2["Core 2 (App Worker/Render)"]
            Core3["Core 3 (Reserved by OS / CapUnlocker)"]
            L1["L1 Cache: 32KB I + 32KB D per Core"]
            L2["L2 Cache: 2MB Unified Shared"]
        end
        subgraph "GPU: PowerVR SGX543MP4+"
            USSE["4 Cores USSE2 (222 MHz)"]
            TBDR["Tile-Based Deferred Rendering (TBDR)"]
        end
    end

    subgraph "Memory Subsystem"
        RAM["Main RAM: 512 MiB LPDDR2"]
        CDRAM["VRAM (CDRAM): 112 MiB Dedicated"]
        SYS_VRAM["OS Reserved VRAM: 16 MiB"]
    end

    Core0 & Core1 & Core2 & Core3 --> L1 --> L2 --> RAM
    USSE --> TBDR --> CDRAM

docs.title: 1. The CPU (ARM Cortex-A9 MPCore)
docs.text: The PlayStation Vita features an ARM Cortex-A9 32-bit quad-core processor (ARMv7-A architecture). - Default Sony Clock: 333 MHz (underclocked out of the factory to preserve battery). - Maximum Native Clock: 444 MHz / 500 MHz (safely unlocked via code or plugins like PSVshell). - Caches: 32 KiB L1 instruction + 32 KiB L1 data cache per core; 2 MiB unified shared L2 cache. - Floating Point Unit: Hardware VFPv3-D32 and 128-bit SIMD NEON engine. - The 4th Core: Reserved by default for VitaOS system background services. Using GrapheneCt's CapUnlocker kernel plugin, homebrew applications can claim this core by setting affinity mask 0x80000 via sceKernelChangeThreadCpuAffinityMask().

docs.title: 2. The GPU (PowerVR SGX543MP4+)
docs.text: A 4-core PowerVR Series5XT graphics chip clocked up to 222 MHz, utilizing a Tile-Based Deferred Rendering (TBDR) pipeline. - The GPU breaks the screen into 16x16 pixel tiles, performing Hidden Surface Removal (HSR / Early-Z) before fragment shading occurs, conserving massive amounts of memory bandwidth.

docs.title: 3. Main Memory vs Video Memory (CDRAM)
docs.text:
Physically, the Vita has two distinct memory buses and partitions:

Memory Partition Physical Size Usable by Homebrew Role and Characteristics Main RAM 512 MiB ~300 MiB to 420 MiB System RAM accessible by CPU. Houses code, heap, the loaded .so binary, decompressed assets, and the FalsoJNI runtime. CDRAM (VRAM) 128 MiB 112 MiB Ultra-fast VRAM directly tied to the GPU bus. Used for framebuffers, active textures, vertex and index buffers. System VRAM 16 MiB 0 MiB Reserved by VitaOS for LiveArea UI and system overlays.

docs.title: 💡 What is the SoLoader Technique?
docs.text: Most emulators interpret alien CPU instructions or translate them dynamically via a JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler. The SoLoader technique is neither an emulator nor a recompiler.

docs.title: Why does Android ARMv7 execute NATIVELY on PS Vita?
docs.text:
Both the PlayStation Vita and 2010–2016 era Android smartphones share the exact same Instruction Set Architecture: ARMv7-A (32-bit) with Thumb-2 instructions and VFP/NEON.

When a game is built for Android using the Android NDK in C++, the compiler outputs an ELF shared library: libgame.so. That binary contains raw, bare-metal ARM machine instructions.

Platform CPU ISA Binary Format Calling Convention Android 32-bit ARMv7-A (Cortex-A8/A9/A15) ELF32 (.so) AAPCS (ARM Architecture Procedure Call Standard) PlayStation Vita ARMv7-A (Cortex-A9 MPCore) ELF32 / Sony SELF (eboot.bin) AAPCS (with softfp / hardfp ABI matching)

Because the PlayStation Vita CPU inherently understands the ARM opcodes in the Android .so, the Vita executes the game's code directly on bare-metal silicon with ZERO CPU emulation overhead.

sequenceDiagram
    participant APK as Android APK (libgame.so)
    participant Loader as Vita Loader (eboot.bin)
    participant FalsoJNI as FalsoJNI Bridge
    participant VitaGL as vitaGL (OpenGL ES)
    participant VitaOS as Vita OS / Hardware

    Loader->>Loader: Reads ELF, allocates RWX block with sceKernelAllocMemBlock
    Loader->>Loader: Processes relocations (R_ARM_RELATIVE, R_ARM_GLOB_DAT)
    Loader->>Loader: Links imported symbols to Loader functions
    Loader->>FalsoJNI: Initializes simulated JVM & JNIEnv
    Loader->>APK: Invokes JNI_OnLoad / nativeInit
    APK->>FalsoJNI: Calls Android Java API (CallStaticVoidMethod)
    FalsoJNI-->>APK: Returns valid simulated response (safe active stub)
    APK->>VitaGL: Draws geometry (glDrawElements)
    VitaGL->>VitaOS: Issues native SCE GXM hardware commands

docs.title: The Loader as the Guest Operating System
docs.text:
If instructions are natively compatible, why can't we run the .so directly? Because the .so expects an Android/Linux runtime environment: 1. It expects Android's standard C library (Bionic libc), with Linux syscalls like open(), mmap(), pthread_create(). 2. It expects Android's display surface (EGL / SurfaceView / OpenGL ES). 3. It expects audio via OpenSL ES, AudioTrack, or SoundPool. 4. It expects a living Java Virtual Machine (Dalvik / ART) responding to JNI calls.

The SoLoader (compiled into your Vita eboot.bin) provides that bridge: - It maps the ELF code and data segments into Vita memory. - It adjusts all absolute pointers using the ARM relocation table. - It intercepts imported functions (malloc, memcpy, glDrawArrays) and routes them to VitaSDK and vitaGL. - It supplies FalsoJNI, a lightweight C runtime that answers all Java queries (device model, storage paths, keyboard inputs, audio state) without running an actual Java VM.

docs.title: 01. Environment & Toolchains
docs.text: Developing and debugging an Android-to-PS Vita port requires a cross-compilation toolchain on your host development workstation (Linux, macOS, or WSL on Windows), reverse engineering suites, and specific kernel bridge plugins installed on physical hardware.

docs.title: 1. VitaSDK (Official Community Toolchain)
docs.text: VitaSDK is the GCC-based cross-compilation suite (arm-vita-eabi-gcc) for PlayStation Vita.

docs.title: Quick Installation (Linux / macOS):
docs.text:
export VITASDK="$HOME/vitasdk"
export PATH="$VITASDK/bin:$PATH"

git clone https://github.com/vitasdk/vdpm.git
cd vdpm
./bootstrap-vitasdk.sh
./install-all.sh

Ensure variables are added to your shell profile (~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc): 

export VITASDK="$HOME/vitasdk"
export PATH="$VITASDK/bin:$PATH"

Verify your setup: 

arm-vita-eabi-gcc --version
# Should output: arm-vita-eabi-gcc (VitaSDK ...)

docs.title: 2. Mandatory Community Libraries (vdpm)
docs.text:
Install foundational porting packages: 

vdpm vitaGL
vdpm mathneon
vdpm libvorbis
vdpm libogg
vdpm openal
vdpm zlib

docs.title: 3. Reverse Engineering Tools
docs.text:
To inspect APK contents and analyze native shared libraries:

  • jadx (Decompiles DEX bytecode into clean Java source):
  • macOS: brew install jadx
  • Linux: Download from jadx GitHub Releases.
  • Docker + devrvk/so-decompiler (Headless Ghidra): Generates readable pseudo-C from any ARMv7 .so via CLI: 
    docker pull devrvk/so-decompiler
  • VitaSDK Binary Utilities:
  • arm-vita-eabi-objdump: Disassembler with full Thumb-2 and ARM ELF support.
  • arm-vita-eabi-nm: Symbol extractor.
  • arm-vita-eabi-readelf: ELF header, dynamic segment, and relocation inspector.

docs.title: 4. psvita-toolkit CLI
docs.text:
A production CLI designed for end-to-end port management: 

# Verify host development dependencies
psvita-toolkit doctor

# Build with CMake presets
psvita-toolkit build --preset debug

# Instant eboot.bin deployment via FTP
psvita-toolkit deploy --eboot --yes

docs.title: 🎮 Required Kernel Plugins on PS Vita
docs.text: For VitaOS to execute dynamically mapped userspace code, the following kernel plugins must be loaded in ur0:tai/config.txt:

docs.title: 1. kubridge (by TheFloW)
docs.text: Repository: github.com/TheOfficialFloW/kubridge Why it's essential: By default, VitaOS userland applications are prevented by W^X protections from creating memory blocks with simultaneous Read, Write, and Execute (RWX) permissions. kubridge exposes kernel services like kuKernelAllocMemBlock, allowing the loader to allocate executable memory for the .so image.

docs.title: 2. fd_fix (by TheFloW)
docs.text:
Repository: github.com/TheOfficialFloW/fd_fix Why it's essential: Prevents kernel crashes when an application closes duplicate or invalid POSIX file descriptors, ensuring standard I/O semantics match Android's Bionic behavior.

# Add to ur0:tai/config.txt
*KERNEL
ur0:tai/kubridge.skprx
ur0:tai/fd_fix.skprx

[!CAUTION] Attempting to boot an SoLoader port without kubridge.skprx active will cause an immediate crash or black screen on launch before the game's first instruction executes.

docs.title: 02. APK Triage & Viability Analysis
docs.text: Before writing code or scaffolding a CMake project, performing an initial feasibility triage on the APK is critical. Evaluating the binary up-front saves weeks of dead-end engineering.

docs.title: 📦 APK Anatomy
docs.text:
An .apk file is a standard ZIP archive. You can unpack it or inspect its contents directly:

game.apk (ZIP)
├── AndroidManifest.xml        # Binary manifest (Java package, GLES version, permissions)
├── classes.dex                # Dalvik executable bytecode for Java classes
├── assets/                    # Game assets (models, textures, audio tracks, levels)
├── res/                       # Android UI layouts and application icons
├── lib/                       # COMPILED NATIVE SHARED LIBRARIES (.so)
│   ├── armeabi/               # ARMv5/v6 binaries (32-bit, soft-float)
│   ├── armeabi-v7a/           # ARMv7-A binaries (32-bit, Thumb-2, VFPv3/NEON) [IDEAL]
│   ├── arm64-v8a/             # ARMv8 binaries (64-bit) [DIRECTLY INCOMPATIBLE]
│   └── x86/                   # Intel x86 binaries [INCOMPATIBLE]
└── META-INF/                  # APK cryptographic signatures

docs.title: 🔍 Criterion 1: Architecture Compatibility (ABI)
docs.text:
Inspect the lib/ directory inside the APK:

unzip -l game.apk "lib/*"
ABI Folder Verdict Technical Reality on PS Vita lib/armeabi-v7a/ OPTIMAL (Ideal) 32-bit ARMv7 code with Thumb-2 and NEON SIMD vectorization. Exactly matches the Vita's Cortex-A9 CPU. lib/armeabi/ COMPATIBLE 32-bit ARMv5TE/v6 code with soft-float arithmetic. Runs natively on Vita because ARMv7 is a strict superset of ARMv6. lib/arm64-v8a/ INCOMPATIBLE (32-bit) 64-bit AArch64 instructions. The PS Vita is strictly a 32-bit machine. If the APK only contains 64-bit binaries, search for an earlier release of the game (pre-August 2019, when Google mandated 64-bit binaries). lib/x86/ / lib/x86_64/ INCOMPATIBLE Intel/AMD instruction sets.

docs.title: 🎨 Criterion 2: Graphics API (OpenGL ES)
docs.text: The PS Vita hardware GPU supports OpenGL ES 1.1 and OpenGL ES 2.0 via vitaGL.

docs.title: Detecting the OpenGL ES Version:
docs.text:
1. Inspect AndroidManifest.xml via jadx: Look for glEsVersion:
  2. 0x00010000 / 0x00010001: OpenGL ES 1.0 / 1.1 (Fixed function pipeline).
  3. 0x00020000: OpenGL ES 2.0 (Programmable vertex and fragment shaders).

  4. 0x00030000+: OpenGL ES 3.0+. Caution: Hardware GLES3 features like transform feedback or 3D textures are not natively available on the Vita GPU.

  5. Inspect imported symbols in .so: 

    objdump -T lib/armeabi-v7a/libgame.so | grep -E "gl(Vertex|Color|CreateShader|Uniform)"

  6. If glVertexPointer, glColorPointer, glMatrixMode appear: OpenGL ES 1.1. Handled with extreme speed by vitaGL's fixed-function pipeline.
  7. If glCreateShader, glCompileShader, glUniformMatrix4fv appear: OpenGL ES 2.0. Uses vitaGL's programmable shader pipeline.
  8. If vkCreateInstance, vkCreateDevice appear: Vulkan. The Vita has no Vulkan driver. Unless an OpenGL ES fallback exists, the port is not viable.

docs.title: 🔗 Criterion 3: NDK Dependencies
docs.text:
Check the external shared libraries needed by the game:

arm-vita-eabi-readelf -d lib/armeabi-v7a/libgame.so | grep NEEDED

Standard dependencies and their Vita status:

Dependency Status Handling on PS Vita libc.so, libm.so, libdl.so Supported Routed directly to VitaSDK Newlib functions. libGLESv1_CM.so / libGLESv2.so Supported Routed to vitaGL. liblog.so Supported Routed to Vita logging (sceClibPrintf / file log). libz.so Supported Linked against zlib from VitaSDK. libOpenSLES.so Supported Reimplemented using sceAudio or OpenAL-Soft. libunity.so / libmono.so Complex Older Unity titles with Mono are possible; modern IL2CPP ARMv7 games often exceed the Vita's 512MB RAM budget.

docs.title: 🚦 Viability Decision Matrix
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Start["Selected APK"] --> CheckArch{"Has lib/armeabi-v7a or armeabi?"}
    CheckArch -- No --> Fail1["❌ Inviable (64-bit or x86 only)"]
    CheckArch -- Yes --> CheckGL{"Graphics API?"}

    CheckGL -- Vulkan Only --> Fail2["❌ Inviable (No Vulkan on Vita)"]
    CheckGL -- GLES 1.1 / 2.0 --> CheckRAM{"Estimated Active RAM Footprint?"}

    CheckRAM -- "> 400 MB active assets" --> WarnRAM["⚠️ High Risk: OOM (Out Of Memory in 512MB RAM)"]
    CheckRAM -- "< 250 MB active assets" --> CheckCode{"Engine implementation?"}

    CheckCode -- "100% Java (classes.dex) with no native C/C++" --> Fail3["❌ Inviable for SoLoader (No native binary)"]
    CheckCode -- "Native C/C++ engine in .so" --> Success["✅ VIABLE: Proceed to Static Analysis"]

docs.title: 03. Static Analysis & Reverse Engineering
docs.text: Static analysis is the systematic process of dissecting the APK's Java bytecode and native .so binaries without executing them, identifying lifecycle hooks, exported methods, and underlying data structures.

docs.title: ☕ Phase 1: Java Decompilation with jadx
docs.text:
Run jadx to decompile the APK's DEX bytecode into Java source:

jadx -d decompiled_apk game.apk

docs.title: 1. Locate the Main Activity
docs.text:
Open decompiled_apk/resources/AndroidManifest.xml and find the activity handling android.intent.action.MAIN:

<activity android:name="com.gameloft.android.GAND.GloftSPAW.ML.HeroOfSparta">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER"/>
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

docs.title: 2. Search for native Method Declarations
docs.text:
Inspect the Activity and related rendering classes (GameRenderer, GLSurfaceView, NativeApp) inside decompiled_apk/sources/. Look for the native keyword:

public class GameRenderer implements GLSurfaceView.Renderer {
    public static native void nativeInit(int width, int height);
    public static native void nativeRender();
    public static native void nativeResize(int width, int height);
    public static native void nativeDone();
    public static native boolean nativeOnTouch(int action, float x, float y, int pointerId);
    public static native boolean nativeOnKeyDown(int keyCode);
}

[!IMPORTANT] These native declarations are the exact entry points your Vita loader will invoke in main.c to drive game initialization, input polling, and frame rendering.

docs.title: 🧩 Phase 2: Dynamic Symbol Extraction (.so)
docs.text: Use binary utilities to inspect exported functions in the .so:

docs.title: 1. List Exported JNI Functions
docs.text:
Standard JNI C naming conventions replace Java package dots . with underscores _: 

objdump -T lib/armeabi-v7a/libgame.so | grep "Java_"

Example output: 

00045a10 g    DF .text  00000034 Java_com_gameloft_android_GameRenderer_nativeInit
00045a50 g    DF .text  00000120 Java_com_gameloft_android_GameRenderer_nativeRender
00045b80 g    DF .text  00000088 Java_com_gameloft_android_HeroOfSparta_nativeOnTouch

docs.title: 2. Check for JNI_OnLoad
docs.text:
objdump -T lib/armeabi-v7a/libgame.so | grep JNI_OnLoad
- If JNI_OnLoad is present: The game registers its native methods dynamically via RegisterNatives(). Your loader must call JNI_OnLoad(&jvm, NULL) during startup. - If JNI_OnLoad is absent: Sockets and methods are statically mapped to Java_package_class_method exports. You can resolve their addresses directly with so_resolve(&so_mod, "Java_...").

docs.title: 🧠 Phase 3: Headless Ghidra Decompilation with Docker
docs.text:
To analyze function logic and struct definitions without running a heavy GUI, use devrvk/so-decompiler:

mkdir -p decompiled_so/libgame_armv7
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$(pwd)/lib/armeabi-v7a:/input" \
  -v "$(pwd)/decompiled_so/libgame_armv7:/output" \
  devrvk/so-decompiler decompile /input/libgame.so /output

This outputs: 1. out_ghidra.c: The entire binary reconstructed in pseudo-C. 2. out_ghidra.h: Inferred types, struct layouts, and prototypes. 3. out_angr.c: Symbolic execution graphs.

Search out_ghidra.c for key functions: 

grep -n "nativeRender" decompiled_so/libgame_armv7/out_ghidra.c

docs.title: ⚡ Phase 4: Disassembly with -M force-thumb
docs.text:
Over 95% of Android ARMv7 game binaries use the Thumb-2 instruction set (mixed 16-bit and 32-bit opcodes) for code density.

[!CAUTION] If you disassemble Thumb-2 code with standard system objdump, it defaults to 32-bit ARM mode and decodes corrupt, nonsensical instructions.

Always disassemble using the VitaSDK toolchain with -M force-thumb:

arm-vita-eabi-objdump -d -M force-thumb \
  --start-address=0x00045a10 \
  --stop-address=0x00045b80 \
  lib/armeabi-v7a/libgame.so

Output: 

   45a10:   b580        push    {r7, lr}
   45a12:   af00        add     r7, sp, #0
   45a14:   f240 102c   movw    r0, #300
   45a18:   f2c0 0004   movt    r0, #4
   45a1c:   6800        ldr     r0, [r0, #0]
   45a1e:   b910        cbnz    r0, 45a26
   45a20:   f7ff fffe   bl      0 <init_subsystem>
   45a24:   bd80        pop     {r7, pc}

docs.title: 📝 Documenting in PORTING_PLAN.md
docs.text: Summarize all findings in PORTING_PLAN.md at your project root: - Identified Java package names and Title ID. - Selected .so binary path and size. - Exported JNI methods and unresolved imports. - Lifecycle methods (init, render, pause, resume, touch).

docs.title: 04. SoLoader Core & Relocations
docs.text: The core of an Android-to-PS Vita port is the userspace dynamic ELF loader (so_util.c or dynlib.c). It fulfills the role of Android's system linker (/system/bin/linker), mapping the shared library into executable memory and wiring up symbols.

docs.title: 🏗️ In-Memory ELF Loading Mechanics
docs.text:
Android NDK .so files are standard 32-bit ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) binaries for the ARM architecture.

flowchart TD
    A["Read .so from ux0:data/"] --> B["Validate ELF Header (Elf32_Ehdr)"]
    B --> C["Calculate Total Memory Footprint (PT_LOAD segments)"]
    C --> D["Allocate RWX Memory Block with sceKernelAllocMemBlock"]
    D --> E["Copy Segments to Memory & Zero-out BSS"]
    E --> F["Process Relocations (.rel.dyn & .rel.plt)"]
    F --> G["Link Imported Symbols to Loader Functions (Hooking)"]
    G --> H["Flush Instruction Cache (sceKernelSyncCacheRange)"]
    H --> I["Binary Execution Ready"]

docs.title: 1. Validating the ELF Header (Elf32_Ehdr)
docs.text: The loader validates the magic identification bytes and machine architecture: - Magic: 0x7F 'E' 'L' 'F' - Class: ELFCLASS32 (1) - Endianness: ELFDATA2LSB (1) - Machine: EM_ARM (40)

docs.title: 2. Allocating RWX Memory
docs.text:
The loader scans the Program Headers (Elf32_Phdr), locates PT_LOAD segments, computes the aligned memory range, and allocates a single executable block:

SceUID memid = sceKernelAllocMemBlock(
    "game_code_block",
    SCE_KERNEL_MEMBLOCK_TYPE_USER_RWX, // Read, Write, and Execute permissions
    aligned_total_size,
    NULL
);

void *base_addr;
sceKernelGetMemBlockBase(memid, &base_addr);

[!NOTE] The ability to allocate USER_RWX memory blocks requires the kubridge kernel plugin. Without it, VitaOS enforces strict W^X memory protection and denies execution.

docs.title: 🔄 The ARM Relocation Engine
docs.text:
Because shared libraries are compiled as Position-Independent Code (PIC/PIE), internal addresses are offsets that must be adjusted by adding the base load address (base_addr).

The loader reads the .rel.dyn and .rel.plt relocation tables:

typedef struct {
    Elf32_Addr r_offset; // Memory address to patch
    Elf32_Word r_info;   // Relocation type and symbol index
} Elf32_Rel;

#define ELF32_R_SYM(val)  ((val) >> 8)
#define ELF32_R_TYPE(val) ((val) & 0xff)

docs.title: Critical ARM Relocation Types:
docs.text: Relocation Code Symbolic Name Loader Action 23 R_ARM_RELATIVE *(uint32_t*)(base + r_offset) += (uint32_t)base; Rebases an internal absolute pointer relative to the new base address. 21 R_ARM_GLOB_DAT Resolves the external symbol name in .dynstr, finds its address (in VitaSDK or the loader), and writes it to *(uint32_t*)(base + r_offset). 22 R_ARM_JUMP_SLOT Targets the PLT (Procedure Linkage Table). Writes the function target address. 2 R_ARM_ABS32 Adds the symbol's runtime value to the existing data at the target offset.

docs.title: 🪝 Symbol Hooking and Routing
docs.text:
When the game calls standard functions like malloc, fopen, or glTexImage2D, the loader intercepts them via a symbol table:

typedef struct {
    const char *symbol;
    uintptr_t func;
} DynLibSymbol;

static const DynLibSymbol dynlib_symbols[] = {
    // Standard libc
    { "malloc", (uintptr_t)&malloc },
    { "free", (uintptr_t)&free },
    { "memcpy", (uintptr_t)&memcpy },
    { "memset", (uintptr_t)&memset },

    // Redirected POSIX I/O
    { "fopen", (uintptr_t)&vita_fopen },
    { "fclose", (uintptr_t)&fclose },

    // Hardware graphics (vitaGL)
    { "glViewport", (uintptr_t)&glViewport },
    { "glClear", (uintptr_t)&glClear },
    { "glDrawElements", (uintptr_t)&glDrawElements },

    // Android logging redirected to console
    { "__android_log_print", (uintptr_t)&vita_log_print },
    { NULL, 0 }
};

docs.title: 🩹 In-Memory Patching & Cache Coherency
docs.text: To bypass incompatible Android services (licensing checks, analytics, anti-tamper hooks), patch the opcodes in RAM:

docs.title: Immediate Return Patch (BX LR):
docs.text:
• Thumb Mode: Write movs r0, #0 (0x2000) and bx lr (0x4770): 
    *(uint16_t *)(so_base + offset) = 0x2000;
*(uint16_t *)(so_base + offset + 2) = 0x4770;
  • ARM Mode: Write mov r0, #0 (0xe3a00000) and bx lr (0xe12fff1e).

docs.title: Mandatory Cache Synchronization
docs.text:
After writing relocations or applying patches, the CPU Data Cache (D-Cache) holds the changes, but the Instruction Cache (I-Cache) may still contain stale code.

[!CRITICAL] Flush the instruction cache after applying relocations and patches: 

sceKernelSyncCacheRange(target_address, size);

docs.title: 05. FalsoJNI & Java Bridge
docs.text:
On Android, games written in C/C++ interface with the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) via JNI (Java Native Interface) to query system locale, read device parameters, access storage paths, and play videos.

Because the PlayStation Vita lacks a full Dalvik/ART virtual machine, we use FalsoJNI: a lightweight C simulation that responds to game queries directly in native C.

docs.title: 🏛️ JNI Function Dispatch
docs.text:
When the game calls JNI, it invokes function pointers inside JNIEnv*:

graph LR
    subgraph "Standard Android"
        AppCpp["Game C++ (.so)"] -->|env->CallStaticIntMethod| JNIEnv["JNIEnv* Dispatch Table"]
        JNIEnv -->|RPC Call| JVM["Dalvik / ART VM (Java)"]
    end

    subgraph "FalsoJNI on PS Vita"
        AppVita["Game C++ (.so)"] -->|env->CallStaticIntMethod| FakeEnv["FalsoJNI Table"]
        FakeEnv -->|Direct C Dispatch| Handler["C Handler Function (falso_jni.c)"]
    end

docs.title: The Simulated Interface Table
docs.text:
FalsoJNI populates a static JNINativeInterface struct matching the JNI standard:

static const struct JNINativeInterface fake_jni_native_interface = {
    .GetVersion = &fake_GetVersion,
    .FindClass = &fake_FindClass,
    .GetMethodID = &fake_GetMethodID,
    .GetStaticMethodID = &fake_GetStaticMethodID,
    .CallVoidMethod = &fake_CallVoidMethod,
    .CallStaticVoidMethod = &fake_CallStaticVoidMethod,
    .CallStaticIntMethod = &fake_CallStaticIntMethod,
    .CallStaticBooleanMethod = &fake_CallStaticBooleanMethod,
    .CallStaticObjectMethod = &fake_CallStaticObjectMethod,
    .NewStringUTF = &fake_NewStringUTF,
    .GetStringUTFChars = &fake_GetStringUTFChars,
    .ReleaseStringUTFChars = &fake_ReleaseStringUTFChars,
};

const struct JNINativeInterface *fake_env = &fake_jni_native_interface;
JNIEnv *env = (JNIEnv *)&fake_env;

docs.title: 🔡 JNI Method Signatures
docs.text:
When a game calls GetMethodID(env, clazz, "methodName", "(signature)returnType"), the signature string encodes argument and return types:

Character Java Type C / C++ Type Z boolean jboolean (uint8_t: 0 or 1) B byte jbyte (int8_t) C char jchar (uint16_t UTF-16) S short jshort (int16_t) I int jint (int32_t) J long jlong (int64_t) F float jfloat (float) D double jdouble (double) V void void Ljava/lang/String; String (Object) jstring (object pointer) [I Array of ints (int[]) jintArray [B Array of bytes (byte[]) jbyteArray

docs.title: 🪤 The Stubbing Trap: Dangerous No-Ops vs Active Stubs
docs.text: One of the most insidious bugs in mobile porting is implementing empty no-op stubs returning 0 or NULL.

docs.title: The Video / Ad Black Screen Hang
docs.text:
Suppose the Android game executes this Java logic on startup: 

public static void playIntroVideo() {
    VideoPlayer.play("intro.mp4", new OnVideoCompletionListener() {
        public void onCompletion() {
            nativeOnVideoCompleted(); // Informs the C++ native engine
        }
    });
}

If you stub playIntroVideo with an empty no-op: 

// ❌ WRONG (Hangs the game permanently):
void fake_playIntroVideo(void) {
    return;
}

The native C++ state machine enters STATE_WAITING_FOR_VIDEO. Because the stub does nothing, nativeOnVideoCompleted() is never invoked. Result: The game hangs permanently on a black screen.

docs.title: ✅ The Solution: Active Stubs
docs.text:
An active stub immediately triggers the callback the engine is waiting for:

// ✔️ CORRECT (Progresses the game loop):
void fake_playIntroVideo(void) {
    sceClibPrintf("[FalsoJNI] playIntroVideo called -> Firing completion callback\n");
    if (nativeOnVideoCompleted_ptr) {
        nativeOnVideoCompleted_ptr(fake_env, NULL);
    }
}

docs.title: 🔤 String Handling and Heap Management
docs.text:
When the game calls GetStringUTFChars, manage memory lifecycle carefully to prevent heap leaks:

const char *fake_GetStringUTFChars(JNIEnv *env, jstring str, jboolean *isCopy) {
    if (!str) return NULL;
    if (isCopy) *isCopy = JNI_TRUE;
    return strdup((const char *)str);
}

void fake_ReleaseStringUTFChars(JNIEnv *env, jstring str, const char *chars) {
    if (chars) {
        free((void *)chars); // Mandatory cleanup
    }
}

docs.title: 06. Graphics Pipeline with vitaGL
docs.text:
The PlayStation Vita hardware features a PowerVR SGX543MP4+ GPU, but Sony's official operating system exposes a proprietary low-level API named SCE GXM. Rewriting an Android game's entire rendering engine to use raw GXM command buffers would require months of effort.

Instead, the community relies on vitaGL by Rinnegatamante: a translation library that wraps OpenGL ES 1.1 and 2.0 calls directly into hardware-accelerated SCE GXM commands with minimal overhead.

docs.title: 🚀 Initialization and Game Loop
docs.text:
In main.c, initialize vitaGL before executing native engine rendering routines:

#include <vitaGL.h>

void init_graphics(void) {
    // vglInitExtended(flags, width, height, ram_buffer_size, msaa_mode)
    // 6 MB vertex command buffer
    vglInitExtended(0, 960, 544, 6 * 1024 * 1024, SCE_GXM_MULTISAMPLE_NONE);

    // Enable VBlank synchronization for tear-free 60 FPS
    vglWaitVblankStart(GL_TRUE);
}

void game_loop_frame(void) {
    // 1. Invoke game's native render function
    nativeRender_func();

    // 2. Swap vitaGL display buffers
    vglSwapBuffers(GL_FALSE);
}

docs.title: 🎨 Graphics Backends Comparison
docs.text: Backend Advantages Trade-offs Use Case vitaGL (Recommended) Open-source, battle-tested, complete GLES 1.1/2.0 coverage, on-the-fly GLSL compiler, optimized for CDRAM. Slight floating-point variance on highly exotic shaders. Standard de facto for 98% of mobile ports. PVR_PSP2 Leaked official PowerVR driver from Sony SDK. Strict GLES 2.0 conformance. Closed source, copyright/licensing issues, rigid integration. Edge-case games with shaders that fail under vitaGL. Raw SCE GXM Maximum theoretical throughput, direct ring buffer control. Extreme complexity: no GLSL support, manual primitive sync. Ground-up native PS Vita engines only.

docs.title: 🪄 Shaders: Translating GLSL to Cg / GXP
docs.text: The Vita GPU requires compiled binary shaders in Sony's GXP format.

docs.title: Runtime vs Offline Transpilation
docs.text:
vitaGL translates GLSL strings to GXM intermediate representations dynamically at runtime. For heavy shaders or to avoid runtime frame drops, use offline AST transpilation:

psvita-toolkit shader-transpile --dump-dir assets/glsl --out-dir assets/cg
This tool uses glslangValidator to compile GLSL to SPIR-V, spirv-cross to generate NVIDIA Cg, and psp2cgc to emit pre-compiled .gxp binaries.

docs.title: 1. Upside-Down FBO Rendering (Y-Flipping)
docs.text:
In standard OpenGL, (0,0) is located at the bottom-left corner. In GXM and some mobile FBO implementations, (0,0) corresponds to the top-left. If rendered textures appear flipped:

// Invert orthographic projection matrix in shaders or adjust viewport:
glViewport(0, 0, 960, 544);

docs.title: 2. Dark Halos on Transparent Sprites (Premultiplied Alpha)
docs.text:
If text rendering or UI textures display black artifacts around transparent edges, the engine uses Premultiplied Alpha: - Replace: glBlendFunc(GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA); - With: glBlendFunc(GL_ONE, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA);

graph LR
    Tex["PNG Texture with Alpha"] --> CheckBlend{"Dark halo around borders?"}
    CheckBlend -- Yes --> PreMult["Enable Premultiplied Alpha: glBlendFunc(GL_ONE, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA)"]
    CheckBlend -- No --> Standard["Standard Blending: glBlendFunc(GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA)"]

docs.title: 3. CDRAM Exhaustion (112 MiB VRAM Limit)
docs.text: vitaGL places textures into high-speed CDRAM by default. If a game exceeds 112 MiB of textures, memory allocation fails. - Direct non-critical textures to main RAM or downsample textures larger than 1024x1024.

docs.title: 07. Audio Subsystem
docs.text:
On Android, audio playback is typically handled by three mechanisms: 1. OpenSL ES: Low-level native C audio API. 2. AudioTrack / SoundPool (Java): Android SDK classes for cached sound effects. 3. MediaPlayer (Java): Android SDK class for streaming background music (OGG, MP3).

On PlayStation Vita, all audio converges into the kernel's sceAudioOut API or higher-level libraries like OpenAL-Soft.

docs.title: 🔊 Audio Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Android Layers in Game"
        Music["Music (MediaPlayer / OGG)"]
        SFX["Sound Effects (SoundPool / OpenSL ES)"]
    end

    subgraph "Loader Abstraction Layer"
        Vorbis["libvorbisfile Decoder"]
        OpenAL["OpenAL-Soft (Context & Buffers)"]
        DirectPCM["Circular PCM Buffer"]
    end

    subgraph "PS Vita Hardware"
        SceAudio["sceAudioOutOutput()"]
        DAC["Stereo Speakers / 3.5mm Headphone Jack"]
    end

    Music --> Vorbis --> OpenAL
    SFX --> OpenAL
    OpenAL --> DirectPCM --> SceAudio --> DAC

docs.title: 1. Direct PCM Output via sceAudioOut
docs.text:
VitaOS manages audio ports via sceAudioOut:

#include <psp2/audioout.h>

static int audio_port = -1;

void init_audio_hardware(void) {
    // Open stereo BGM port at 44100 Hz with 1024 sample buffer
    audio_port = sceAudioOutOpenPort(
        SCE_AUDIO_OUT_PORT_TYPE_BGM,
        1024,
        44100,
        SCE_AUDIO_OUT_MODE_STEREO
    );

    // Set 100% volume
    int vol[2] = { 32768, 32768 };
    sceAudioOutSetVolume(audio_port, SCE_AUDIO_VOLUME_FLAG_L_CH | SCE_AUDIO_VOLUME_FLAG_R_CH, vol);
}

void output_pcm_block(const int16_t *samples) {
    // Blocks until 1024 samples are consumed by hardware
    sceAudioOutOutput(audio_port, samples);
}

docs.title: 📻 Background Music Streaming (OGG Vorbis)
docs.text:
Link libvorbisfile for streaming compressed background music:

#include <vorbis/vorbisfile.h>

typedef struct {
    OggVorbis_File vf;
    FILE *f;
    int is_playing;
    int loop;
} BGMStream;

BGMStream bgm;

void bgm_play(const char *filepath, int loop) {
    bgm.f = fopen(filepath, "rb");
    if (!bgm.f) return;

    if (ov_open_callbacks(bgm.f, &bgm.vf, NULL, 0, OV_CALLBACKS_DEFAULT) < 0) {
        fclose(bgm.f);
        return;
    }

    bgm.loop = loop;
    bgm.is_playing = 1;
}

int audio_thread(SceSize args, void *argp) {
    int16_t pcm_buffer[2048]; // 1024 stereo samples
    int bitstream;

    while (1) {
        if (bgm.is_playing) {
            long bytes = ov_read(&bgm.vf, (char *)pcm_buffer, sizeof(pcm_buffer), 0, 2, 1, &bitstream);
            if (bytes > 0) {
                sceAudioOutOutput(audio_port, pcm_buffer);
            } else if (bytes == 0 && bgm.loop) {
                ov_time_seek(&bgm.vf, 0); // Loop
            }
        } else {
            sceKernelDelayThread(10000);
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 🧩 FalsoJNI SoundPool Emulation
docs.text:
When games trigger sounds via SoundPool.play(...):

jint fake_SoundPool_play(JNIEnv *env, jobject obj, jint soundID, jfloat leftVolume, jfloat rightVolume, jint priority, jint loop, jfloat rate) {
    play_openal_sound_effect(soundID, leftVolume, loop);
    return soundID; // Return valid stream ID (> 0) to signal success
}

[!TIP] If SoundPool.play returns 0, the Android engine assumes audio hardware failure and may attempt to reload the sound file every frame, causing massive stutter.

docs.title: 08. Controls & Input Mapping
docs.text: Translating touch-first smartphone controls to the ergonomic inputs of the PlayStation Vita requires handling both front/rear capacitive touch surfaces and physical controls (D-Pad, action buttons, dual analog sticks).

docs.title: 🎮 Polling Hardware Controls in VitaOS
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "PS Vita Hardware"
        FrontTouch["Front Capacitive OLED/LCD"]
        BackTouch["Rear Touchpad"]
        Buttons["Physical Buttons (D-Pad, Cross, Square, L/R)"]
        Sticks["Dual Analog Sticks"]
    end

    subgraph "VitaOS APIs"
        sceTouch["sceTouchPeek(SCE_TOUCH_PORT_FRONT)"]
        sceCtrl["sceCtrlPeekBufferPositive()"]
    end

    subgraph "Loader Abstraction Layer"
        Sanitizer["Touch ID Sanitizer (Prevents Heap Corruption)"]
        TouchMapper["Physical-to-Touch Synthetic Mapper"]
        Deadzone["Analog Deadzone Filter"]
    end

    subgraph "Game Engine"
        NativeTouch["nativeOnTouch(action, x, y, id)"]
        NativeKey["nativeOnKeyDown(keyCode)"]
    end

    FrontTouch --> sceTouch --> Sanitizer --> NativeTouch
    Buttons --> sceCtrl --> TouchMapper --> NativeTouch
    Buttons --> sceCtrl --> NativeKey
    Sticks --> sceCtrl --> Deadzone --> TouchMapper

docs.title: 1. Mandatory Touch Sampling Initialization
docs.text:
By default in VitaOS, touch sampling is disabled to save power. Without enabling it, sceTouchPeek will always report zero touches:

#include <psp2/touch.h>

void init_touch_system(void) {
    sceTouchSetSamplingState(SCE_TOUCH_PORT_FRONT, SCE_TOUCH_SAMPLING_STATE_START);
    sceTouchSetSamplingState(SCE_TOUCH_PORT_BACK, SCE_TOUCH_SAMPLING_STATE_START);
}

docs.title: 💣 The Touch Report ID Heap Corruption Trap
docs.text: This is one of the most elusive causes of random crashes in mobile ports:

docs.title: The Problem:
docs.text:
Sony's SceTouchReport struct exposes a hardware-assigned id: 

SceTouchData touch;
sceTouchPeek(SCE_TOUCH_PORT_FRONT, &touch, 1);
uint8_t raw_id = touch.report[i].id; // Can be 15, 48, 120...

Android engines (like Cocos2d-x or Gameloft engines) allocate a fixed-size internal array for active fingers: 

// Internal C++ game engine code:
Touch active_touches[5];

void onTouchDown(int pointer_id, float x, float y) {
    active_touches[pointer_id].x = x; // ❌ CRASH IF pointer_id > 4
}

If you pass Sony's raw report.id (e.g. 15) to the engine: The engine accesses &active_touches[15], writing out of bounds and silently corrupting the application heap. The game will not crash immediately, but will abort minutes later during unrelated heap operations.

docs.title: ✅ The Solution: Virtual Pointer ID Pool
docs.text:
Map raw hardware touch IDs to contiguous virtual slots between 0 and 3:

#define MAX_TOUCH_SLOTS 4

static int virtual_touch_slots[MAX_TOUCH_SLOTS] = { -1, -1, -1, -1 };

int get_virtual_touch_id(int sony_raw_id) {
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_TOUCH_SLOTS; i++) {
        if (virtual_touch_slots[i] == sony_raw_id) return i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_TOUCH_SLOTS; i++) {
        if (virtual_touch_slots[i] == -1) {
            virtual_touch_slots[i] = sony_raw_id;
            return i;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

void release_virtual_touch_id(int sony_raw_id) {
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_TOUCH_SLOTS; i++) {
        if (virtual_touch_slots[i] == sony_raw_id) {
            virtual_touch_slots[i] = -1;
            break;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 🕹️ Mapping Physical Buttons to On-Screen Touch
docs.text:
For mobile games without controller support:

#include <psp2/ctrl.h>

typedef struct {
    uint32_t vita_button;
    float screen_x;
    float screen_y;
    int is_pressed;
} VirtualButton;

static VirtualButton v_buttons[] = {
    { SCE_CTRL_CROSS,    860.0f, 440.0f, 0 }, // Attack
    { SCE_CTRL_SQUARE,   780.0f, 380.0f, 0 }, // Jump
    { SCE_CTRL_TRIANGLE, 840.0f, 300.0f, 0 }, // Menu
};

void process_touch_emulation(uint32_t current_buttons) {
    for (int i = 0; i < sizeof(v_buttons)/sizeof(v_buttons[0]); i++) {
        VirtualButton *vb = &v_buttons[i];
        int pressed = (current_buttons & vb->vita_button) != 0;

        if (pressed && !vb->is_pressed) {
            nativeOnTouch(0, vb->screen_x, vb->screen_y, 9 + i); // ACTION_DOWN
            vb->is_pressed = 1;
        } else if (!pressed && vb->is_pressed) {
            nativeOnTouch(1, vb->screen_x, vb->screen_y, 9 + i); // ACTION_UP
            vb->is_pressed = 0;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 🎯 Analog Stick Deadzone Filtering
docs.text:
Vita analog sticks report unsigned bytes 0..255 centered at 128:

#define ANALOG_DEADZONE 30

void read_analog_stick(uint8_t raw_x, uint8_t raw_y, float *out_x, float *out_y) {
    int dx = (int)raw_x - 128;
    int dy = (int)raw_y - 128;

    if (abs(dx) < ANALOG_DEADZONE) dx = 0;
    if (abs(dy) < ANALOG_DEADZONE) dy = 0;

    *out_x = (float)dx / 128.0f;
    *out_y = (float)dy / 128.0f;
}

docs.title: 09. File System & Asset Management
docs.text: The PlayStation Vita storage topology and partitioning schemes differ significantly from standard Android Linux environments. Properly mapping paths and configuring asset packages (.apk/.obb) ensures your game locates its models, audio, textures, and save files.

docs.title: 💾 Storage Topology
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "VitaOS Partitions"
        UX0["ux0: (Primary Memory Card / SD2Vita)"]
        APP0["app0: (Read-only mount of current app)"]
        UR0["ur0: (System memory / taiHEN plugins)"]
    end

    subgraph "Loader Path Translation"
        AndroidPath["Android Path: /sdcard/Android/data/com.game/"]
        VitaDataPath["Target Path: ux0:data/my_game/"]
    end

    AndroidPath -->|sanitize_path()| VitaDataPath
    VitaDataPath --> UX0
    APP0 -->|Contains eboot.bin & LiveArea| UX0

docs.title: Partition Roles:
docs.text:
• app0: (Read-Only): Where the app package is installed (ux0:app/<TITLEID>/). Contains eboot.bin and LiveArea data. Writing to app0: triggers an immediate permission error.
  • ux0:data/<game>/ (Read-Write): The standard homebrew location for game data files, saved states (saves/), and runtime log files (logs/).

docs.title: 🔀 POSIX Path Redirection
docs.text:
Mobile games hardcode Linux filesystem paths: - /sdcard/Android/data/com.gameloft.spaw/files/... - /data/data/com.gamevil.zenonia3/...

Intercept standard I/O calls (fopen, open, stat, mkdir):

#define DATA_PATH "ux0:data/heroofsparta/"

char *sanitize_path(const char *path, char *out_path, size_t max_len) {
    if (!path) return NULL;

    if (strncmp(path, "ux0:", 4) == 0 || strncmp(path, "app0:", 5) == 0) {
        strncpy(out_path, path, max_len);
        return out_path;
    }

    const char *p = path;
    if (strncmp(p, "/sdcard/", 8) == 0) p += 8;
    else if (strncmp(p, "/storage/emulated/0/", 20) == 0) p += 20;
    else if (*p == '/') p++;

    snprintf(out_path, max_len, "%s%s", DATA_PATH, p);
    return out_path;
}

FILE *vita_fopen(const char *filename, const char *mode) {
    char clean_path[1024];
    sanitize_path(filename, clean_path, sizeof(clean_path));
    return fopen(clean_path, mode);
}

docs.title: 📦 Asset Packaging Strategies
docs.text: Strategy Advantages Drawbacks 1. Unpacked Loose Files Easy to inspect and mod textures/music directly. FAT32 cluster slack (32KB/64KB per cluster) wastes hundreds of megabytes on games with thousands of small files. 2. In-Memory APK/OBB (ZIP) Saves massive space; single compressed archive. Faster sequential card reads. Requires engine ZIP support (e.g. Cocos2d-x CCFileUtils) or linking libzip / minizip.

docs.title: 🔠 Case Sensitivity (FAT vs ext4)
docs.text:
• Android (ext4): Strict case-sensitive paths (Texture.PNG != texture.png).
  • PS Vita (FAT32 / exFAT): Case-preserving, but case-insensitive lookups.

[!WARNING] If the APK contains two files differentiated only by casing in the same directory (e.g. icon.png and ICON.PNG), copying them to the Vita will overwrite one with the other. Check for collisions if assets appear corrupted.

docs.title: 10. LiveArea & VPK Packaging
docs.text: The final distributable package for PlayStation Vita is a .vpk archive. A VPK is a standard ZIP containing the signed executable (eboot.bin), metadata (sce_sys/param.sfo), and the visual shell resources (LiveArea).

docs.title: 🖼️ LiveArea Asset Specifications
docs.text:
Sony's system shell (SceShell) strictly enforces image resolutions, formats, and file size limits:

Asset Resolution (Pixels) Maximum Allowed Size Role on Console icon0.png 128 x 128 128 KiB Circular home screen application bubble. startup.png 280 x 158 64 KiB Interactive startup gate button. bg0.png 840 x 500 128 KiB LiveArea gate background image. pic0.png 960 x 544 256 KiB Optional full-screen background banner.

docs.title: 🚫 The Infamous 0x8010113D Installation Error
docs.text:
Error 0x8010113D in VitaShell or the system installer occurs when LiveArea images violate Sony's internal specifications:

flowchart TD
    PNG["LiveArea PNG Asset"] --> CheckDims{"Exact pixel dimensions?"}
    CheckDims -- No --> Fail1["❌ Error 0x8010113D (Wrong Dimensions)"]
    CheckDims -- Yes --> CheckSize{"File size under KiB limit?"}
    CheckSize -- No --> Fail2["❌ Error 0x8010113D (File Too Large)"]
    CheckSize -- Yes --> CheckFormat{"8-bit Indexed Palette?"}
    CheckFormat -- No --> Fail3["❌ Error 0x8010113D (32-bit RGB Interlaced)"]
    CheckFormat -- Yes --> Success["✅ Valid LiveArea Asset"]

docs.title: Golden Rules for LiveArea Images:
docs.text:
1. 8-bit Indexed Palette (256 colors): Always quantize PNGs using pngquant or ImageMagick.
  2. No Interlacing: The hardware decoder does not support interlaced/progressive PNG formats.
  3. Automate with psvita-toolkit: 
    psvita-toolkit livearea --auto extras/livearea/ --validate

docs.title: 🍏 The macOS AppleDouble ._* Trap
docs.text:
When packaging on macOS, the OS generates hidden AppleDouble metadata files (._icon0.png, ._param.sfo, ._eboot.bin) on FAT32/exFAT drives.

[!CAUTION] If ._* files are packaged inside the .vpk, VitaShell installation fails or displays corrupted app bubbles.

Clean junk files before packaging: 

find . -name "._*" -type f -delete
# Or:
psvita-toolkit clean-junk

docs.title: 📜 Generating param.sfo
docs.text:
Configure your Title ID and display name with vita-mksfoex:

vita-mksfoex -s TITLE_ID="PSVHOS001" "Hero of Sparta" param.sfo

docs.title: Title ID Format:
docs.text:
• Exactly 9 uppercase alphanumeric characters.
  • Standard homebrew format: PSV followed by 3–4 letters and digits (e.g. PSVHOS001, ZENONIA02).

docs.title: 📦 Automated Packaging via CMake
docs.text:
In CMakeLists.txt:

vita_create_self(eboot.bin ${PROJECT_NAME})

vita_create_vpk(${PROJECT_NAME}.vpk ${TITLE_ID} eboot.bin
    VERSION "01.00"
    NAME "${GAME_NAME}"
    FILE extras/livearea/icon0.png sce_sys/icon0.png
    FILE extras/livearea/startup.png sce_sys/livearea/contents/startup.png
    FILE extras/livearea/bg0.png sce_sys/livearea/contents/bg0.png
    FILE extras/livearea/template.xml sce_sys/livearea/contents/template.xml
)

docs.title: 11. Crash Triage & Hardware Debugging
docs.text: When a port crashes on physical hardware, there is no need to guess. The Triangulation Methodology combines three authoritative sources of truth to pinpoint the exact line of code: 1. The flushed runtime log (fflush). 2. The kernel core dump (.psp2dmp) parsed via vita-parse-core. 3. The .so binary disassembled with arm-vita-eabi-objdump -M force-thumb, cross-referenced with Ghidra pseudo-C and jadx Java source.

docs.title: 🎯 The Triangulation Workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Crash["💥 Hardware Crash"] --> Step1["1. Read Last Line of game.log"]
    Step1 --> Step2["2. Fetch .psp2dmp via FTP"]
    Step2 --> Step3["3. Parse Dump with vita-parse-core & loader.elf"]
    Step3 --> Step4{"Where does PC (Program Counter) point?"}

    Step4 -- "Inside .so memory space" --> FramePC["Relevant Frame = PC (Direct .so Crash)"]
    Step4 -- "Inside SceLibKernel or Loader" --> FrameLR["Relevant Frame = LR (Corrupted argument passed to syscall)"]

    FramePC & FrameLR --> Step5["4. Compute Offset inside .so"]
    Step5 --> Step6["5. Locate Nearest Symbol with objdump / nm"]
    Step6 --> Step7["6. Disassemble with objdump -M force-thumb"]
    Step7 --> Step8["7. Match with Ghidra Pseudo-C"]
    Step8 --> Fix["🔧 Exact Line Found -> Patch or Register Stub"]

docs.title: 📋 Step 1: Flushed Logs
docs.text:
Always call fflush(log_file) after every log write so that buffered text is committed to flash storage before a panic:

void vita_log(const char *fmt, ...) {
    va_list args;
    va_start(args, fmt);
    vfprintf(log_file, fmt, args);
    fflush(log_file);
    va_end(args);
}

Check the final log line: - If GetStaticMethodID(..., "checkLicensing", ...) is the last entry: register the missing JNI stub. - If a missing asset path is reported: update path sanitization.

docs.title: 🔬 Step 2: Parsing .psp2dmp Core Dumps
docs.text:
Upon encountering a Data Abort, VitaOS generates a crash dump in ux0:data/ or ur0:temp/core/ named psp2core-XXXXXXXXXX-eboot.bin.psp2dmp.

Parse it with vita-parse-core against your debug loader.elf (the unstripped ELF with symbols):

python3 vita-parse-core/main.py crash.psp2dmp build/loader.elf

Output: 

Exception Type: Data abort (read access to 0x00000004)
Registers:
  r0: 0x00000000   r1: 0x98124000   r2: 0x00000001   r3: 0x81005a20
  PC: 0x98045a1c   LR: 0x98045a05   SP: 0x810ff400

docs.title: ⚖️ Step 3: Deciding Between PC and LR
docs.text:
• If PC lies within .so memory (0x98000000+): The crash instruction was executed inside the game's native library. Investigate that offset.
  • If PC lies within SceLibKernel or the loader (eboot.bin): LR (Link Register) is the caller! The game code invoked a system function (e.g. memcpy or fopen) with an invalid parameter (NULL pointer or corrupt size). Inspect the call-site in LR.

docs.title: 🔎 Step 4: Resolving the Offset & Matching Disassembly
docs.text:
Calculate: offset = PC - so_base_address (e.g. 0x98045a1c - 0x98000000 = 0x45a1c).

Find the enclosing function: 

objdump -T libgame.so | grep -v UND | awk '{print $1, $NF}' | sort > syms.txt
Locate the symbol with the highest address <= 0x45a1c. Assume it resolves to GameRenderer_updateUI + 0x24.

Disassemble with -M force-thumb: 

arm-vita-eabi-objdump -d -M force-thumb --start-address=0x459f8 --stop-address=0x45a30 libgame.so


   45a18:   6808        ldr     r0, [r1, #0]    ; Read pointer from r1
   45a1a:   2800        cmp     r0, #0          ; Check if NULL
   45a1c:   6840        ldr     r0, [r0, #4]    ; ❌ Crash: r0 is NULL, attempts to read offset +0x4!

Match with Ghidra's out_ghidra.c: 

if (player_controller != NULL) {
    player_controller->health_bar->update();
}
player_controller was valid, but its health_bar sub-object was NULL because the UI layout had not been initialized in FalsoJNI.

docs.title: ⚠️ ARMv7 Memory Alignment Traps
docs.text:
On x86 PCs, unaligned memory accesses are transparently handled by CPU microcode. On the ARM Cortex-A9 CPU of the PS Vita, LDRD (Load Register Dual, 64-bit), STRD, and NEON vector instructions (VLD1) trigger an instant hardware Data Abort if the address is not aligned to 8 or 16 bytes.

[!TIP] If a crash occurs on an ldrd r2, r3, [r0] instruction with non-NULL registers, check r0. If the address ends in 0x4 rather than 0x0 or 0x8, a struct is misaligned in memory. Enforce 8-byte alignment via memalign(8, size).

docs.title: 12. Real Engine Archaeology
docs.text: Across more than 30 production PlayStation Vita ports, recurring architectural patterns emerge. This chapter catalogs real-world engine analyses, quirks, and battle-tested solutions.

docs.title: ⚔️ Family 1: Classic Gameloft Engines (2010–2013)
docs.text:
Representative titles: Hero of Sparta, Dungeon Hunter 2, N.O.V.A. 2, Shadow Guardian, Eternal Legacy, Six-Guns, Gangstar Rio, Brothers in Arms 2, Asphalt 5 & 6.

graph TD
    subgraph "Gameloft Native Architecture"
        GameSO["lib<game>.so (Core Logic, Renderer, Physics)"]
        StormSO["libStormGLOFT.so (Anti-Tamper & Licensing)"]
    end

    subgraph "Core Subsystems"
        ResLoader["GLResLoader (Package & Asset Manager)"]
        Media["GLMediaPlayer (Music & Sound Effects)"]
        Renderer["GameRenderer (GLES Loop)"]
    end

    GameSO --> ResLoader
    GameSO --> Media
    GameSO --> Renderer
    StormSO -.->|Ignored on Vita| GameSO

docs.title: Critical Quirks:
docs.text:
1. The libStormGLOFT.so Companion: Gameloft APKs typically bundle libStormGLOFT.so alongside the main game library. It serves as an anti-tamper stub without useful exports. Only load the primary game .so.
  2. GLResLoader Asset Resolution: Gameloft uses a multi-tier asset loader:
  3. Call GLResLoader_nativeInit(int) before rendering.
  4. Assets are searched across resolution directories (1024x768, 960x540, 800x480).
  5. Universal JNI Signatures:
  6. Java_..._GLMediaPlayer_nativeInit
  7. Java_..._GameRenderer_nativeInit(width, height, orientation)
  8. Java_..._GameRenderer_nativeRender()

docs.title: 🛡️ Family 2: Gamevil Nexus2 / Clet Engine
docs.text:
Representative titles: Zenonia 2, Zenonia 3, Zenonia 4, Destinia, ILLUSIA 1 & 2, Advena.

graph LR
    subgraph "Java ME to Clet Native Evolution"
        BytecodeMIDP["Original J2ME Logic (16-bit tiles)"] --> Clet["Clet C++ Runtime"]
        Clet --> Nexus2["Nexus2 Engine"]
        Nexus2 --> GLES["GLES1 Fixed Function Pipeline"]
    end

docs.title: Critical Quirks:
docs.text:
1. MIDP / Java ME Heritage: Originally developed for Korean feature phones, Gamevil wrapped their micro-edition engines into C++ runtimes (Clet / Nexus2) for Android.
  2. Shared Symbol Layout: Zenonia 2 and Zenonia 3 share 95% of their JNI exports: Java_com_gamevil_nexus2_Natives_nativeInit and Java_com_gamevil_nexus2_Natives_nativeEvent.
  3. Character Encoding: Strings frequently use EUC-KR or UTF-8 without BOM. When rendering with stb_truetype, sanitize input to standard UTF-8.

docs.title: 🏹 Family 3: Com2uS Engines
docs.text: Representative titles: Inotia 2: A Wanderer of Luone, Inotia 3: Children of Carnia, Inmortal Dusk.

docs.title: Critical Quirks:
docs.text:
• Mach-O (iOS) vs ELF (Android): Certain Com2uS titles had superior HD releases on iOS. In titles like Inotia 2, loading decrypted 32-bit ARMv7 Mach-O binaries directly with a custom Mach-O loader is viable, wrapping CoreAudio and UIKit calls into C and vitaGL.
  • Audio Channels: Audio buffers are 22050 Hz mono PCM; expand to stereo before feeding sceAudioOutOutput.

docs.title: 🌳 Family 4: Cocos2d-x Engines
docs.text: Representative titles: Badland 2, Rayman Jungle Run, The Impossible Game.

docs.title: Critical Quirks:
docs.text:
• Standardized entry point: Java_org_cocos2dx_lib_Cocos2dxRenderer_nativeInit(width, height).
  • Asset streaming via CCFileUtils: points to ux0:data/<game>/game.apk and streams assets from ZIP directly in RAM.

docs.title: 13. AI-Assisted Porting Guide
docs.text:
Developing SoLoader ports involves substantial boilerplate code (JNI tables, symbol maps, audio wrappers) paired with deep low-level debugging.

This guide outlines best practices for human + AI pair programming (using Antigravity, Claude, GPT), optimizing context tokens and preventing reverse-engineering hallucinations.

docs.title: ⚡ Context and Token Economy
docs.text:
Ghidra pseudo-C (out_ghidra.c), disassemblies (objdump), and decompiled Java sources can easily exceed 500,000 tokens.

graph TD
    BigFiles["Massive Files (out_ghidra.c: 50MB, jadx classes)"] --> Filter["Targeted Shell Filters (grep, objdump -T, awk)"]
    Filter --> Subagent["Lightweight Subagent / Local Script"]
    Subagent --> Context["Main Reasoning Context (< 10,000 tokens)"]
    Context --> Solution["Architectural Decision / Exact C Patch"]

docs.title: Golden Rules:
docs.text:
1. Never dump full out_ghidra.c files into chat: Use grep -n -C 15 "function_name" to extract only the 30 lines under active investigation.
  2. Delegate mechanical boilerplate to fast models: Use lightweight subagents (Flash / Flash-Lite) for formatting symbol tables and stub scaffolding, reserving deep reasoning models for .psp2dmp crash triage.

docs.title: 🛡️ Preventing Reverse-Engineering Hallucinations
docs.text: AI models will invent plausible JNI method names or return types if context is underspecified. Prevent this with strict grounding:

docs.title: 1. Always provide verbatim signatures from Java or objdump
docs.text:
❌ Vague Prompt: "Write a stub for the sound function in Hero of Sparta."

✔️ Grounded Prompt: "jadx decompilation reveals this exact Java declaration: public static native int nativePlayMusic(String path, boolean loop); Write the C FalsoJNI function with signature (Ljava/lang/String;Z)I, convert jstring to UTF-8, route it to our audio backend, and return streamID > 0 to indicate success."

docs.title: 2. Verify Primitive Type Mappings
docs.text: Ensure the AI strictly uses: - Z = jboolean (1 byte). - J = jlong (64-bit signed integer). - Never return stack pointers for object or string queries.

docs.title: 📋 Batch Stubbing Prompt Template
docs.text:
You are an expert PS Vita port engineer using FalsoJNI.
The game logged the following missing Android methods:

1. com.gameloft.android.GLUtils.getDeviceModel() -> Ljava/lang/String;
2. com.gameloft.android.GLMediaPlayer.isMusicActive() -> Z
3. com.gameloft.android.GLResLoader.openAsset(String path) -> [B

Requirements:
1. Write the corresponding C function with matching FalsoJNI signatures.
2. For strings, return fake_NewStringUTF with a safe value ("PlayStation Vita").
3. For booleans, return JNI_TRUE or JNI_FALSE according to expected game behavior.
4. Output the jni_methods registration table entries.

docs.title: Getting Started with PSVita Homebrew Development
docs.text:
Autor: gl33ntwine (Vitaliy Atamanenko) Fecha de publicación original: 2 de Mayo de 2022 Tiempo de lectura: ~38 min (6,918 palabras) URL original (sitio inactivo): https://gl33ntwine.com/posts/develop-for-vita/ Captura archivada en Wayback Machine: Web Archive (2024-12-06) Licencia: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)

Hi there! If you landed here, I probably don’t need to tell you about how amazing the PlayStation Vita is and how sad it is that Sony failed its marketing and threw it away so quickly. Nevertheless, I feel obliged to say that the Vita is also very curious from a developer’s perspective.

You must understand that a portable console released in 2012 can’t possibly have the capabilities of a PlayStation 4, and in most cases—not even of a PlayStation 3. But the limits of this tiny old handheld hardware are still more of a challenge than an annoyance in 2022. I do believe that if you take time to master your gamedev techniques with PSV, making smooth and optimized software for any desktop, mobile, or console platform will be much less of a problem for you.

And most importantly, the Vita homebrew scene is still cherished by maintainers and developers, brimming with new libraries, languages, engines, and whatnot. Of course, that also implies a not-that-small crowd of faithful players who will enjoy and value your works.

Convinced now? :) Let’s get into it.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This guide is planned to consist of several parts, starting with general information and Vita SDK in the first part and getting to other programming languages, engines, plugins, and Android ports in the following parts.

Keep in mind that Vita SDK is a C/C++ toolchain. So, to develop things using Vita SDK directly, you need to have some knowledge of either of these languages and a good understanding of computer science in general. Don’t leave just yet if you don’t know both C and C++, though! This article will also contain a lot of information that can prove helpful, no matter the language or engine you end up using. Feel free to use the navigation on the right to jump to the sections you’re interested in the most.

[!TIP] Running any homebrew applications on the Vita requires custom firmware. If you don’t know what it is or are ready to close the article now, don’t worry. It’s a straightforward and safe process and even a completely reversible one. You can always “un-hack” your device back like it never happened. More info: https://vita.hacks.guide/

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
As you can see on the diagram above, controls-wise, the Vita is pretty much a DualShock 4 gamepad with a 5-inch touchscreen in the front and its touchpad moved to the back. Some important differences to note are that analog sticks can’t be clicked, and you don’t have the second pair of triggers (L2/R2 on DS4), just L/R.

The good news here is that everything you see on the diagram can be accessed from Vita SDK. Except for maybe the accessory port. Not sure why it even exists :)

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
PlayStation Vita sports an ARM Cortex-A9. Thankfully, Sony chose the convenient, optimized, and well-known ARM architecture for the Vita instead of the rather exotic MIPS they had used for the PSP. By the way, this exact CPU was used by Apple for the iPhone 4S and other devices on the Apple A5 SoC.

Vita’s variant of Cortex-A9 has four 500 MHz cores, each with an L1 Instruction Cache of 32 KiB and a Data Cache of 32 KiB. Additionally, all four share a common L2 cache of 2 MiB.

Before you look at your i9-99999k 1337 GHz processor and decide it’s a lost cause, let me remind you that the PlayStation 2 CPU was clocked at 294 MHz and still did a lot of impressive stuff. Also, hey, look at Killzone Mercenary gameplay! Basically, fame clock speed is not everything. Optimization is key!

If you want to dive deeper into the specifics of the Vita’s CPU, I recommend to read:

  • “Main Processor” on the HENkaku Wiki.
  • “CPU” on the PlayStation Developer Wiki.

Here, let’s just focus on two of its caveats important to you as a developer.

docs.title: Overclocking
docs.text:
To be precise, the CPU clock is not 500 MHz; it’s 111 MHz to 500 MHz. This clock speed can be changed on the user’s side using a plugin such as PSVShell:

The standard CPU clock speed is 330 MHz, but the developer can force a higher value in code like this.

Such “overclocking” is safe and won’t cause overheating or unexpected behavior: we’re not actually overclocking but reversing the underclocking introduced by Sony to extend battery life.

docs.title: Fourth core
docs.text:
By default, the fourth core is reserved for system processes and can’t be used by “game applications” (that is, any homebrew applications in our context).

In most cases, your game or application’s performance depends on the single-core clock speed. But if you happen to have a multithreading-intensive task and feel the lack of that fourth core, there is a plugin named CapUnlocker by GrapheneCt.

To make use of the fourth core having CapUnlocker set up, specify 0x80000 for the CPU affinity mask when creating a new thread. You can also use that value with sceKernelChangeThreadCpuAffinityMask() to change the affinity mask of an already existing thread.

Don’t worry if you don’t understand what the last paragraph tells you to do just yet. Just keep in mind that such an option exists.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
While the CPU can be considered rather average, the Vita’s GPU is pretty impressive. It’s a PowerVR Series5XT chip, SGX543MP4+, to be specific. In terms of GFLOPS, it’s 11x more powerful than the PSP, 6x more powerful than Nintendo 3DS, and only 5.5x less powerful than Nintendo Switch!

The GPU has 4 cores, each clocked at up to 222 MHz. Overclocking is done the same way as for CPU, either on a user’s or developer’s side.

If you want to know more in-depth stuff about the GPU, I recommend to read:

  • “SGX543” on the HENkaku Wiki.
  • “Graphics” on the PlayStation Developer Wiki.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
I hope you survived the previous two sections with ease because this one may be tough, but it is still very important.

Physically, there are two kinds of RAM: main memory (512 MiB) and video memory (128 MiB). Let’s start with video memory, which is mainly used—as the name implies—by the GPU.

docs.title: Video memory / VRAM (128 MiB)
docs.text:
Both types of memory are partitioned on the Vita. With VRAM, it’s quite simple:

1) CDRAM: 112 MiB partition. CDRAM is the video memory you can use in your applications. Unless you’re going really low-level, pretty much any graphics library will deal with VRAM for you, e.g., store active textures and geometry and manage it. In most cases, you only have to be mindful of its volume (again, 112MB) to not put 8192x8192 textures in your game. Other than that, just trust your graphics library/API.

2) Reserved: 16 MiB partition. Yes, Sony stole 12.5% of our video memory for system needs. Sigh. Nothing we can do about it.

docs.title: Main memory / RAM (512 MiB)
docs.text:
Main memory is much more heavily partitioned:

1) USER_RW (aka MAIN): 365 MiB partition. This is your best friend. Pretty much everything (except graphics and some system stuff) will use USER_RW memory for storage. An important note here is that by default, USER_RW is 256 MiB to leave room for multitasking. With applications that do not use up the whole maximum of 365 MiB, you can run system apps like Web Browser or Music Player in parallel. Later in this article, I will discuss how to adjust the USER_RW budget in the param.sfo section.

2) PHYCONT: 26 MiB partition. PHYCONT is a physically contiguous memorywhat is it?. On the Vita, it is normally used for things like system video codecs that require this type of memory. But in case you’re out of USER_RW and desperately need to squeeze out some more MiBs, you can use PHYCONT, but keep in mind that it must be 1MiB-aligned. An example of such usage is VitaGL, a PSVita Native Graphics API (GXM) ↔ OpenGL compatibility layer.

3) CDLG: 9 MiB partition. CDLG is a partition normally used by the system for common dialogs, such as on-screen keyboard input dialogs. If you still need to squeeze out more RAM even after using PHYCONT and are sure that you won’t use common dialogs, 8.77 MiB of CDLG is there to help (8.77 due to 1024 alignment). An example of CDLG usage can be found in VitaGL, too.

4) Reserved: 112 MiB partition. The final 112 MiB of RAM is reserved by the operating system for different purposes, such as storing shared modules, kernel, shell, etc. No luck trying to use this.

docs.title: Memory caching and performance
docs.text:
TL;DR:

  • There are UNCACHED and CACHED versions of USER_RW and PHYCONT. “CACHED” means using the CPU’s L1/L2 cache. CDRAM is, of course, always UNCACHED. For best performance on CPU, USER_RW | CACHED is the best way to go, and for GPU, start with CDRAM until filled out and then use UNCACHED variants of other types of RAM. Another reminder here: this info is useful when going really low-level or squeezing out every last bit of performance/RAM. Generally, all this stuff is handled for you.

Not TL;DR:

  • Elaborate memcpy speed test with different implementations and types of memory.
  • More about Memory Budget on the HENkaku wiki

docs.title: Storage and file system
docs.text:
Superficially, it might seem that there’s next to nothing to say about the Vita’s storage. It’s understandable: for a power user, a quick look at the file manager would suffice to understand that everything works in a very similar to Windows way; you get a few “disks”/partitions for different system purposes and a typical file/directory tree inside them:

But as always, there are some things you need to understand about it.

docs.title: Storage performance
docs.text:
The Vita’s storage is arguably its least performant part. Developers often had to invent ways to deal with abysmal loading times while porting or creating something, all while experiencing no CPU or GPU performance issues.

The Baba Is You port is a prime example. While average Android users didn’t notice anything strange, the initial version of the port took 40 minutes to load into the main menu. Another 20 was needed to load the map, and another 20 was needed to finally load into the level. You can tell I’m telling the truth by the eye twitch I got that day.

The exact reason for that was that while loading assets, the engine tried to open tens of thousands of non-existing files, and while it looks like it’s free on Android, it very much wasn’t on the Vita. Just by adding a static list of really existing files and searching it before actually trying to access the file system, we brought down these loading times to mere seconds.

Unfortunately, it doesn’t even matter what kind of storage medium you use: whether it’s the internal memory, memory card, SD2Vita (by the way, do get one if you haven’t yet!), external HDD/SSD/pen drive, or even Wi-Fi or Ethernet. It’s going to be slow. Do keep that in mind and try to optimize your IO access as much as possible. Especially if you’re dealing with directories with many files; in that case, either pack them in an archive or at least split the files across several directories.

IO access speed can be improved by using a Fios2 caching layer and some more performant IO calls, but that’s a topic for a separate article.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
The partition you will work with 99% of the time is ux0. This is where the OS stores the installed games data, and this is where we put our homebrew applications as well. Most often, it would be mapped to SD2Vita (a normal MicroSD inserted into the game card slot via an adapter), but sometimes it can be the Memory Card or internal storage, so do be mindful not to waste too much disk space for users.

In the later sections of this article, we will touch on ux0:/app and ux0:/data, the two most important directories to you as a developer.

If you want to learn more about how the file system works and what you can find there, check out these links:

  • “File Management” on the HENkaku Wiki.
  • “Partitions” on the PlayStation Developer Wiki.
  • “Files on the PS Vita” on the PlayStation Developer Wiki.

docs.title: What is VitaSDK
docs.text:
Vita SDK is an open-source toolchain for PlayStation Vita development. Don’t be surprised just yet: of course, Sony didn’t open-source anything. The community has progressively built this SDK by analyzing and reverse-engineering Vita’s firmware.

The term “Toolchain” in the above paragraph refers to a set of development tools, such as a compiler, linker, libraries, etc., that enable you to build your code so that you can run it on the Vita and use its platform-specific features, like touchscreen or gyroscope.

Vita SDK is built on top of well-known open-source software like GCC, so if you’ve made something for Linux-like platforms before, you’ll quickly get the hang of it.

In the last few years, Vita SDK’s POSIX compliance what is it? reached the point that unless you’re using Vita-specific hardware features like proximity sensors, your code can be fully cross-platform. For example, in my osu! client, the only target platform checks in the code are for back touchpad input and overclocking, like here. Thus, it can be compiled for desktop platforms as-is.

Another way to give you a general idea of how similar our current toolchain is to a normal Linux toolchain is to say that it is not uncommon for the process of porting SDL-poweredwhat is it? C/C++ games to the Vita to consist of just minor edits to the Makefile/CMakeListswhat is it? and adjusting the inputs code and screen resolution.

docs.title: VitaSDK and Sony SDK — any difference?
docs.text:
Don’t confuse Vita SDK (or “VitaSDK”, “vitasdk”) with the official Sony PSVita SDK, often referred to as “sce sdk”, “official sdk” or “sony sdk”.

The official SDK is licensed, copyrighted software provided by Sony to its registered developers. It is likely illegal to download or use it if you weren’t granted permission directly by Sony. Theoretically, you could even be sued for that, even though the community has never heard of such cases.

Unless you’re up for obscure things nobody in the scene did before, it’s highly unlikely that you will ever need to replace Vita SDK with SCE SDK. Personally, I can’t remember any homebrew that required it to be developed from the top of my head. Well, except for Unity (the game engine) projects, but we’ll get to that in the future parts of the guide.

docs.title: Okay, what about dolcesdk and vdsuite?
docs.text:
I hope your head hasn’t blown yet from the number of SDKs we have :) Those are the last two you should know about.

dolcesdk was a fork of VitaSDK with additions from the leaked official SDK code. It is now deprecated, so if you encounter something using it, you can most likely easily port it to either Vita SDK or vdsuite.

vdsuite is what dolcesdk was deprecated in favor of. vdsuite brings additions and improvements to the official SDK; it’s regularly updated and maintained by the community. As you might have guessed, it is in a rather gray legal area, so use it at your own risk.

You would probably need vdsuite if you wanted to work on anything using ScePaf, which is a Sony library that allows—among other things—to use the native Vita UI widgets (see NetStream, BetterHomebrewBrowser, PSVshellPlus).

In a normal case, Vita SDK is the way to go unless you know that you need some features specific to vdsuite.

docs.title: Setting up Vita SDK
docs.text:
Vita SDK can be easily set up on Linux, macOS, and Windows desktops. ARM64 Raspberry Pi and Apple M1 builds are coming soon™; if you’re using one of these platforms now and don’t know how building toolchains works, you better use another device or wait some time. By the way, some mad lads were even able to run it on a Nokia N900 with postmarketOS :)

The installation process is quite easy. Follow the instructions on the Vita SDK home page and come back here if you’re done or have some issues with environment variables (solving which happens to be the next section).

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
On the page linked above, you can see that one of the required steps is to set the $VITASDK environment variable and add $VITASDK/bin to $PATH like this:

export VITASDK=/usr/local/vitasdk
export PATH=$VITASDK/bin:$PATH # add vitasdk tool to $PATH

What sometimes causes confusion is that the place to set these is not universal. To learn where to put your environment variables, do the following in your terminal:

cd ~ # this will take you to your home directory
ls -d .* # this will show all hidden ("dot") files

For example, on my macOS Monterey, I don’t have either .bash_profile or .bashrc mentioned by Vita SDK. Here is the output of the above commands:

v@mbp ~ % ls -d .*
.CFUserTextEncoding  .DS_Store     .Trash
.bitnami             .bundle       .gitconfig
.gem                 .ghidra       .ssh
.viminfo             .zsh_history  .zshrc

But I do have .zshrc! Zsh is another shell, a replacement for Bash that became the default in macOS a few versions ago. Thus, .zshrc is the place where I should put these lines.

If you have nothing similar to .bash_profile, .bashrc, or .zshrc, try creating a new file named .bashrc and using it instead.

After you’ve done this, restart your Terminal and check if it worked with the following command:

echo $VITASDK # should print whatever you set as the vitasdk path in the variable

If the output of this command is empty no matter what you try, and even googling didn’t help, there is still a last resort, but you’ll have to do this every time you start the terminal:

source ~/.bashrc # or whatever the file you put variables into is named

This will forcefully load the environment variables, and you’re all set to continue the installation.

docs.title: Hello world
docs.text:
Yes, finally, we are ready to do something palpable :) Let’s grab vitasdk/samples from GitHub and build a hello-world application:

cd /your/preferred/working/directory/
git clone https://github.com/vitasdk/samples
cd samples/hello_world
cmake .
make

If you didn’t mess up the installation, this should produce a hello_world.vpk file ready to be run on your Vita. To run it, do the following:

  • Send the generated hello_world.vpk to your Vita:
  • Start an FTP server on your Vita (for example, with VitaShell - by pressing the SELECT button).
  • Upload the .vpk to the Vita using your FTP client (for example, FileZilla or just plain curl)
  • Install the .vpk on your Vita using a VPK installer (for example, with VitaShell - by pressing the X button on the .vpk)

Finally, on your home screen, a new “Hello World” bubble will appear that you can run and behold something like this:

docs.title: Setting up the dev and debug environment
docs.text:
Now, when you learned the basics of Vita’s hardware and SDKs, set up your own copy of Vita SDK, and even built your first application with it, you’re pretty much all set to start developing or porting whatever you want on your own.

But, to make this process a little more mindful than just “editing hello world in Notepad until it becomes a game”, let’s go over several key aspects of it.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Since Vita SDK is a normal C/C++ toolchain, you can write code using whatever you like. Visual Studio Code, Sublime Text, and Notepad++ are some of the most popular choices.

Personally, I prefer JetBrains CLion because of its powerful IDE capabilities like refactoring helpers, fully integrated debugger, clangd, IntelliSense, etc., but it’s paid.

Vita SDK offers a great variety of already ported open source libraries, as well as a pretty good level of POSIX compliance, thus allowing the majority of cross-platform code to run as-is. We will go over some of those libraries and graphics APIs in one of the later sections of this article.

For future reference, in Vita SDK, C Standard Library (libc) is implemented through a newlib port, and C++ Standard Library (libstdc++) is provided by GCC.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Again, since Vita SDK is a normal C/C++ toolchain, you probably can use whatever generator / build system you like that can work with gcc/g++ compilers (even something like Ninja or Meson).

There are two most common choices that will let you find more answers on the internet when needed, as well as save your contributors some time:

  • GNU Make The Standard for many decades, perfect for simple (as in “small” and “easy on dependencies”) projects. Example of a Makefile for a Vita project.
  • CMake More modern alternative to Make, perfect for more complex or crossplatform projects. Example of a CMakeLists.txt for a Vita project.

For this and later articles, I will use only CMake. For me it has more intuintive syntax and lots of helpful macros that easen dependency management and project setup for the Vita specifically.
